  * Natural language commands without rigid phrasing
  * Context awareness across a conversation
  * Control of lights, heating, TVs, cameras and other smart home devices
  * Confirmation before sensitive actions or purchases
  * Optional personalized wake word
  * Strong safety rules for potentially dangerous actions
  * A more proactive assistant experience, while still respecting user control

I often work in a single Codex thread for several hours, with many revisions and replacements of similar material.

In long threads, finding a specific earlier result becomes surprisingly difficult. I may remember roughly when a decision or change was made, but the UI gives me no reliable timestamp to locate it. Codex shows occasional date/time separators and a duration such as “Worked for 58s,” but many separate runs can appear inside one large untimestamped block.

As a result, I repeatedly have to scroll up and down through the thread, reread similar-looking responses, and manually search for the exact iteration I need. This takes a significant amount of time, interrupts the working flow, and becomes increasingly frustrating as the thread grows.

It is especially difficult when I need to reconstruct earlier context or compare several versions of the same text or implementation. The existing periodic timestamps are too sparse to serve as useful navigation landmarks.

Could every completed run show its actual completion time next to the duration?

**Current:**
`Worked for 58s`

**Proposed:**
`Worked for 58s · Completed at 18:21`

I would keep the duration because it is useful, but add the absolute completion time next to it. A compact timestamp, hover tooltip, or optional display setting would all work. Ideally, the full date, time, and time zone would also be accessible.

This is not just a cosmetic improvement. Per-run timestamps would provide stable landmarks inside long threads, reduce the time spent searching and scrolling, and make multi-hour Codex workflows much easier to navigate.

record.text: We gave ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and Claude the same 10 shopping messages to see whether AI could tell a scam from a legitimate transaction.

external.description:
key takeaways

  * All four assistants caught all five scam-control messages.
  * ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude correctly cleared all five legitimate controls; Copilot marked two as uncertain.
  * Scam-risk scores ranged from 78 to 95, while legitimate controls ranged from 5 to 40, with no overlap in this controlled test.
  * AI was most useful for spotting red flags and suggesting checks, not for proving that a seller is genuine.



Imagine you are about to transfer ₦300,000 to an online seller.

The price looks reasonable, but something feels off. The seller wants a bank transfer. Perhaps they are rushing you, the account name doesn't match the business, or they say you cannot inspect the item before paying.

But before pressing send, would pasting that message you receive from said seller into an AI assistant help you determine if you’re about to get scammed?

That matters because AI is already entering the same shopping journey where many Nigerians encounter fraud. Visa's 2026 Stay Secure study found that 88% of Nigerian consumers surveyed used AI to assist with shopping, while 83% bought products through social media. Among respondents who had experienced scams, 57% said it happened on social media.

So, I tested whether four popular AI assistants could recognise warning signs before money changed hands.

**MORE INSIGHTS ON THIS TOPIC:**

  * AI Scams and the New Trust Problem: Why Online Fraud Looks Real
  * Social Media Scams Cost Users $2.1 Billion, Meta Apps Lead Losses
  * What Are Scam Compounds? Everything We Know About the Forced-Labour Cybercrime Factories



## I gave four AIs the same 10 shopping messages

I tested the free versions of ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Claude using 10 controlled messages: five scam controls and five legitimate controls.

They were synthetic, but not arbitrary. I built five matched situations: an Instagram phone purchase, a Facebook Marketplace laptop, a fashion preorder, a parcel-delivery message, and a WhatsApp appliance sale around documented marketplace and payment-scam behaviours.

The scam versions combined cues such as urgent payment demands, personal accounts, surprise fees, blocked inspection, and pressure to transfer before verification.

The legitimate versions deliberately kept normal Nigerian e-commerce behaviours that can look risky in isolation, including WhatsApp ordering, bank transfers, and a preorder deposit, but added safeguards such as inspection, invoices, matching business-account names, refund terms, or payment after checking the item.

I did this because an AI that simply equates "WhatsApp", "bank transfer," or "deposit" with fraud might look cautious while being useless to shoppers.

Each assistant received the same prompt and message in a fresh chat. We asked for a classification: LIKELY SCAM, LIKELY LEGITIMATE, or UNCERTAIN, a 0–100 risk score, up to three reasons, and advice before paying. I also told it not to assume facts outside the message.

The experiment produced 40 responses.

##  How the four AI assistants performed

All four caught every scam-control message. Only Copilot was more cautious on two legitimate controls.

## Every AI caught every scam, but that is not the whole story

Across the 20 scam assessments, every assistant returned LIKELY SCAM. None gave a scam message false reassurance.

That shows all four were good at recognising combinations of clear warning signs. But it does not show that they can detect every real scam.

We deliberately built these cases around recognised cues, so 5/5 is best read as evidence that the assistants notice those cues when they are present.

record.text: Sniper Elite: Resistance, MLB The Show 26, Wobbly Life and Chained Echoes headline PlayStation Plus this September.

external.description:
Sony has revealed the PlayStation Plus Monthly Games for September 2026, and subscribers are getting four games across different genres.

The September lineup includes Sniper Elite: Resistance, MLB The Show 26, Wobbly Life, and Chained Echoes, giving PS Plus members a mix of tactical action, baseball, co-op fun, and classic-style JRPG gameplay.

All four games will be available to PlayStation Plus members from September 1 through October 5, 2026.

Here’s a closer look at the September 2026 PlayStation Plus games.

Phantom Blade Zero State of Play: Everything RevealedDonnie Yen isn’t just choreographing Phantom Blade Zero’s kung fu, he’s now a character in it, and the State of Play just revealed how.TechloyEmmanuel Umahi

## Sniper Elite: Resistance

Platforms: PS5, PS4

Leading the September lineup is Sniper Elite: Resistance, Rebellion's tactical third-person shooter set during World War II.

The game shifts the focus to a hidden war taking place behind enemy lines in occupied France, with its story running parallel to Sniper Elite 5.

As expected from the series, precision shooting, stealth and tactical combat are at the heart of the experience. Players can also take on the campaign in co-op, while the fan-favourite Axis Invasion mode returns, allowing players to invade another player's campaign as an Axis sniper.

PlayStation Plus members will also receive access to an MLB The Show 26 Jump Start Bundle, which includes five The Show Packs, an Equipment Pack and a Jumpstart Choice Pack.

## MLB The Show 26

Platforms: PS5, PS4

Baseball fans are getting their turn with MLB The Show 26, the latest entry in San Diego Studio's long-running baseball franchise. The game lets players build their own baseball career through Road to the Show while also developing their squad in Diamond Dynasty. The inclusion of MLB The Show 26 gives this month's PlayStation Plus lineup a sports option alongside the action and RPG-focused games.

record.text: A simple piece of tape could previously hide Meta's recording indicator. The company is now making the camera shut down when it detects the light has been covered or tampered with.

external.description:
Covertly recording people with smart glasses without their permission has become a growing concern. When Meta launched its first-generation Ray-Ban Stories, the company added a recording LED to let people nearby know when the glasses were capturing photos or videos.

But users soon found a way around it: simply covering the recording light with tape could allow the glasses to look like an ordinary pair of glasses while still recording.

Meta is now moving to close that loophole. The company says its AI glasses will disable the camera when they detect that the capture LED has been blocked or physically tampered with. Meta has also been improving its ability to detect attempts to modify or destroy the LED.

Meta Smart Glasses App May Contain Unreleased Face Recognition CodeA report found a code hidden inside Meta’s smart glasses app, reviving questions about consent, surveillance, and privacy.TechloyOgbonda Chivumnovu

## Why Meta is making the change

The reasoning is fairly simple. As AI glasses become more popular, concerns about people using them to secretly record others are growing.

There have been cases of people using smart glasses to covertly film and harass others in public. Back in February, Techloy reported on Russian man Vladislav Liulkov, who had been accused by the governments of Kenya and Ghana of secretly recording women without their consent, editing the clips, and posting them online.

Instagram has also taken action against creators who post this type of content, but the problem has continued.

There is another problem Meta is trying to address: a market for accessories and services designed to bypass the recording light.
